title: Frequency‐Domain Airborne Electromagnetic Imaging of Permafrost Reveals Heterogeneity and Drivers of Permafrost Change in the Discontinuous Permafrost Zone of Northwestern Canada
abstract: Northern permafrost landscapes are undergoing rapid warming and thaw, yet the three‐dimensional subsurface structure that governs thaw vulnerability and landscape response remains poorly resolved by conventional ground temperature monitoring and satellite remote sensing. Frequency‐domain airborne electromagnetic (AEM) surveys can resolve permafrost structure rapidly at regional scales across complex terrain. Here, we present three representative survey lines from 1,340 line‐km of AEM data collected in the central Mackenzie Valley, Northwest Territories. Rather than relying on fixed resistivity thresholds, we develop a gradient‐based method to identify permafrost depth and transition‐zone thickness from vertical resistivity gradients, enabling consistent mapping across warm (>−2°C) discontinuous permafrost. Interpretations are evaluated using a co‐located electrical resistivity tomography profile and borehole temperature measurements in the context of regional surficial geology mapping. The AEM survey images resistivity to depths of ∼100 m along a linear infrastructure corridor and reveals permafrost thicknesses ranging from absent beneath sufficiently large, deep, or persistent waterbodies to ∼35 m in undisturbed uplands. Results demonstrate pronounced lateral heterogeneity controlled by geology, hydrology, slope position, vegetation cover, and disturbance history. Areas affected by wildfire in the past three decades exhibit persistently reduced shallow resistivity, broadened permafrost‐base transition zones, and locally thinner permafrost, whereas talik networks, including through‐going taliks that fully disrupt permafrost continuity, are resolved beneath sufficiently large, deep, or persistent waterbodies. These findings quantify the subsurface legacy of disturbance and highlight spatial variability and vulnerability within the discontinuous permafrost zone, with implications for infrastructure stability, groundwater connectivity, and future thaw trajectories.

title: Dust Aerosol Effects on Charge Structure and Lightning Activity of a Continental Thunderstorm: A Modeling Study With Thompson‐Electrification Scheme
abstract: A mesoscale electrification‐coupled model was established within the WRF model by integrating with the Thompson microphysics scheme. Based on the Thompson‐electrification scheme and MERRA‐2 aerosol reanalysis data, this study investigated the individual and synergistic impacts of dust aerosols acting as cloud condensation nuclei (cloud condensation nuclei (CCN)) and ice nuclei (IN) on microphysics, charge structures and lightning activity of a rare dust‐associated continental thunderstorm. By four sensitivity experiments, the results demonstrated that elevated CCN concentrations increased the mass content and number concentrations of cloud droplets, whereas high IN significantly amplified ice crystal and snow aggregates concentrations. Combined CCN and IN effects synergistically intensified hydrometeor modifications, the polarity reversal threshold for non‐inductive charging by increasing mixed‐phase liquid water content is lowered with increased CCN, and the charge separation efficiency through ice‐graupel collisions is increased by high IN. Under the influence of dust aerosol, the lower positive charge region is strengthened by CCN enhancement and main charge layer densities are intensified by IN increasing. The charge structure of thunderstorm demonstrated a classical tripole under dust free circumstance, converted to quadrupolar configurations with high dust aerosol increasing, which facilitated +CG lightning generation. In addition, under high CCN concentrations, total cloud‐to‐ground (CG) lightning frequency decreased but the positive CG (+CG) proportion increased, while both CG frequency and +CG proportion increased with high IN concentration, resulting in a maximum prevalence of +CG lightning.

title: Influence of Particle Properties and Grain Size on Aggregation in Dry Particle‐Laden Volcanic Jets
abstract: Explosive volcanic eruptions can inject large amounts of ash into the atmosphere. These suspended particles pose hazards to aircraft, so a better understanding of the ash residence time and transport distance is needed. Fine particles combine to form larger aggregates, altering their settling behavior. Ash aggregation is influenced by liquid bonding, electrostatic forces, and preferential concentration driven by turbulence. We examine particle aggregation through controlled, low‐humidity experiments at similar particle‐fluid scaling to conditions near a volcanic vent. Particle‐laden jets used compressed air containing three types of particles at controlled mass loadings: hollow glass spheres (∼10 μm diameter), solid nickel spheres (∼7 μm diameter), and volcanic ash from the 18 May 1980, Mount St. Helens eruption (<2 mm diameter). The jet had Reynolds numbers from 5,000 to 10,000, with Stokes numbers between 0.6 and 24,000 based on convective timescales and length scales. Flow velocity was measured using particle image velocimetry, and particle fallout was collected and imaged on microscope slides. To reduce errors from particle overlap, we introduce a normalization method that compares experimental images with synthetic images of randomly distributed particles. Results show minimal aggregation for a single particle type, but there is more than 10 times enhanced aggregation when hollow glass and nickel particles are combined. This behavior may be attributed to differential charging of the hollow glass and nickel, which promotes electrostatic attraction. Volcanic ash particles showed modest aggregation, but normalized trends were still challenging to quantify because aggregates and large individual particles overlapped in size.

title: Satellite‐Based Estimates of Irrigation Water Use Versus Modeling Reconstructions: How Much do They Differ?
abstract: Knowing water amounts destined for agricultural practices, essentially consisting of irrigation water use (IWU), is essential for water resources management. Although explicit and consistent information on IWU is generally lacking worldwide, remote sensing and modeling platforms offer valuable solutions for estimating it. The objective of this work is to perform an intercomparison between satellite‐based IWU products and modeling reconstructions over four main irrigation hotspots worldwide: the Contiguous United States (CONUS), the Ebro basin (Spain), India, and the Murray‐Darling basin (Australia). Remote‐sensing‐based IWU estimated through Soil‐Moisture‐Inversion (SM‐Inversion) and SM‐Delta approaches are considered. As modeled data, five Global Hydrological Models are evaluated: H08, PCR‐GLOBWB, WaterGAP, LPJmL, and QUAlloc. Reference irrigation volumes are exploited to assess which source is more reliable. Over CONUS and Murray‐Darling basin, lower discrepancies between data sources (satellite or modeling) are detected. Referring to spatially‐averaged IWU magnitudes, the comparison over CONUS provides RMSE $\text{RMSE}$ ranging from 9.52 to 12.21 mm/month, BIAS $\text{BIAS}$ between 3.24 and 7.06 mm/month, and Pearson correlation (r $r$) from 0.77 to 0.90. The same intervals for the Murray‐Darling basin are 8.04–17.70 mm/month for RMSE $\text{RMSE}$, 4.81–12.63 mm/month for BIAS $\text{BIAS}$, and 0.42–0.85 for r $r$. Consequently, over such areas, similar performances in reproducing actual irrigation amounts by satellite estimates and modeling reconstructions, when available, are found. Over the Ebro basin, where the strongest discrepancies are found, satellite‐based data sets outperform model outputs in reproducing reference data. The lack of in situ observations for India prevents a clear assessment of the results, but insights on differences introduced by parametrizations are established.

title: Alaskan Glaciers in a Warming Climate
abstract: Glaciers across Alaska are undergoing rapid mass loss, with implications for sea‐level rise, natural hazards, water resources, and more. Here, we utilize new snowline and melt extent observations of Alaskan glaciers at high spatiotemporal resolutions to improve projections to 2100. Specifically, we incorporate these observations into the calibration scheme for the large‐scale Python Glacier Evolution Model (PyGEM), and subsequently simulate future changes under various climate scenarios. We estimate that glaciers in Alaska will lose 49 ± 17% to 73 ± 26% of their 2015 mass by the end of the century, depending on the future climate. Nearly all small glaciers (<1 km2) will disappear by 2100 regardless of the climate scenario, along with the smallest glacierized subregions of Alaska, namely, the Brooks and Talkeetna ranges. Across larger subregions, negative mass balance is projected to peak in the middle of the 21st century for the modest future warming scenario (i.e., SSP1‐2.6), while negative mass balance continues to increase to 2100 for the most aggressive future warming scenario (SSP5‐8.5). Much of these changes are attributed to increasing temperatures that cause greater melt in addition to a shift in early‐winter precipitation from snow to rain which reduces accumulation and enhances melt by exposing the underlying ice earlier in the next ablation season. Of the remaining glaciers in 2100, 15%–60%, depending on the future climate, have no accumulation area and are thus committed to disappearance. Overall, the widespread loss of glaciers in Alaska by 2100 has implications on ecology, water resources, natural hazards, and tourism across the region.

title: Age‐Period‐Cohort Analysis of the Global Death Burden of Main Diseases Attributable to High Temperature in the Past 30 Years: Based on the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021
abstract: High temperatures pose a serious threat to human health. Quantifying the main disease death burden attributable to high temperatures can provide scientific evidence for policy development. Using Global Burden of Disease 2021 data, we identified the death burden attributable to high temperatures across all causes and determined the three leading causes. For each, we used age‐standardized mortality rates attributable to high temperature (HA‐ASMR) and estimated temporal trends via age‐period‐cohort modeling at global, regional, and national levels (1990–2021). Ischemic heart disease, stroke, and lower respiratory infections were the top three causes of deaths attributable to high temperature in 2021. Low‐middle Socio‐demographic Index (SDI) regions had the highest HA‐ASMR for ischemic heart disease (3.49, 95%UI: 0.96–6.57) and stroke (2.55, 95%UI: 0.77–5.01), whereas lower respiratory infections showed the highest HA‐ASMR in low SDI regions (2.52, 95%UI: 0.85–4.35). Age‐period‐cohort analysis generated net drift values for HA‐ASMR in high SDI regions, with values of 0.99% (95%CI: 0.60%–1.39%) for ischemic heart disease, 1.19% (95%CI: 0.99%–1.40%) for stroke, and 2.36% (95%CI: 2.01%–2.70%) for lower respiratory infections. Longitudinal age curves showed elevated mortality risks attributable to high temperature in populations over 60 years. Global period and cohort rate ratios for high‐temperature‐attributable ischemic heart disease mortality increased over time. Global ischemic heart disease and stroke deaths attributable to high temperature continued rising with sharply elevated risks in older adults, while lower respiratory infection deaths attributable to high temperature among youth in high‐income countries are increasing. Therefore, adaptation strategies must be specific to disease and age, varying by regional characteristics.

title: Solvent heterogeneity regulates assembly pathways in supramolecular polymerization
abstract:
Supramolecular polymers often require solvent mixtures for their preparation but their impact on supramolecular polymerization remains poorly understood. Here, the authors demonstrate that solvent heterogeneity biases assembly pathways in supramolecular polymerization, with the extent of this effect determined by monomer structure. 
 Supramolecular polymers are fundamental mimics of biological assemblies with diverse functions. However, predicting monomer solubility and controlling the colloidal stability of the resulting assemblies in solution remain major challenges. As a result, their preparation commonly relies on solvent mixtures, which can generate local heterogeneities during sample processing—an effect that remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that solvent heterogeneity biases assembly pathways in supramolecular polymerization, with the extent of this effect modulated by monomer structure. Using an amphiphilic Pd(II) complex as a model system, we uncover a thermally accelerated transition from kinetically controlled discrete nanostructures to thermodynamically stable supramolecular polymers in water/1,4-dioxane mixtures. Combined experimental and theoretical analyses reveal that this transformation is mediated by microscopic liquid–liquid phase separation within the mixed solvent, creating 1,4-dioxane-enriched microdomains with increased local monomer concentration. Thermal annealing enhances molecular mobility and promotes the growth and coalescence of these microdomains, facilitating the transition to one-dimensional fibers. Extending the investigation to structurally related monomers further identifies the metal center and hydrogen-bonding motifs as key design elements governing this behavior. By linking molecular design and solvent heterogeneity to pathway complexity, our findings highlight how mixed solvents can be used to control supramolecular polymerization. Supramolecular polymers often require solvent mixtures for their preparation but their impact on supramolecular polymerization remains poorly understood. Here, the authors demonstrate that solvent heterogeneity biases assembly pathways in supramolecular polymerization, with the extent of this effect determined by monomer structure.

title: Bacteroides–Escherichia interactions contribute to colonization resistance against Clostridioides difficile
abstract:
Here the authors demonstrate that interactions between Bacteroides and Escherichia shape resistance to Clostridioides difficile and identify ecological and metabolic signatures with the potential to guide microbiome-based therapies. 
 Commensal gut bacteria are key contributors to the resilience against pathogen invasion. This is exemplified by the success of faecal microbiota transplantation in treating recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection. Yet, characteristics of communities that can confer colonisation resistance and the underlying mechanisms remain largely unknown. Here we use a synthetic community of 14 commensal gut bacteria to uncover inter-species interactions and metabolic pathways underpinning the emergent resilience against C. difficile invasion. We challenged this synthetic community as well as faecal-matter-derived communities with antibiotic treatment and C. difficile in a continuous flow bioreactor. Using generalised Lotka-Volterra and genome-scale metabolic modelling, we identified interactions between Escherichia coli and Bacteroides/Phocaeicola sp. as key to the pathogen’s suppression. Metabolomics and targeted validation experiments revealed that fructan-derived fructooligosaccharides, vitamin B3 biosynthesis, and competition for Stickland metabolism precursors causally contribute to suppression across multiple C. difficile strains and donor backgrounds. Analysis of metagenomics data from patient cohorts and clinical trials attested the in vivo relevance of the identified metabolic pathways and the ratio between Bacteroides and Escherichia in successful colonisation resistance. The latter was found to be a stronger discriminator than commonly used alpha diversity metrics. Together, our study uncovers emergent microbial interactions in pathogen resistance with implications for rational design of bacteriotherapies. Here the authors demonstrate that interactions between Bacteroides and Escherichia shape resistance to Clostridioides difficile and identify ecological and metabolic signatures with the potential to guide microbiome-based therapies.

title: Molecular architecture of Cryptococcus cell walls reveals species-specific chitosan-dependent remodeling
abstract:
This study reveals distinct cell-wall organization in two pathogenic Cryptococcus species, revealing that chitosan loss triggers species-specific structural remodeling that may influence host interactions. 
 Cryptococcus neoformans and Cryptococcus gattii are fungal pathogens that cause life-threatening infections, including cryptococcal meningitis. A distinctive feature of the cryptococcal cell wall is the extensive deacetylation of chitin to chitosan, a modification that is essential for virulence but whose structural role in cell-wall organization remains poorly understood. Here, we analyze the cell walls of wild-type strains of both species and their avirulent chitosan-deficient mutants, which serve as vaccine candidates. Loss of chitosan disrupted cell morphology and altered cell-wall ultrastructure, with more pronounced defects in C. neoformans. Solid-state NMR reveals that aggregated α-(1→3)-glucans form the principal rigid domain of the cell wall in both species and are closely associated with chitin microfibrils, whereas surrounding β-glucans and mannoproteins constitute a more dynamic matrix. Chitosan modulates hydration and flexibility, and its loss increases chitin exposure and triggers species-specific remodeling of the polysaccharide network. In C. neoformans, chitosan depletion increased α-(1→3)-glucan content and reduced β-glucan levels, whereas C. gattii selectively lost one α-(1→3)-glucan subtype while maintaining β-glucan levels. Although capsule production remained intact, chitosan deficiency altered glucuronoxylomannan linkage patterns and mannoprotein composition. These findings reveal how chitosan organizes cryptococcal cell-wall architecture and highlight distinct structural adaptation strategies among pathogenic Cryptococcus species. This study reveals distinct cell-wall organization in two pathogenic Cryptococcus species, revealing that chitosan loss triggers species-specific structural remodeling that may influence host interactions.

title: Symbiotic nitrogen fixation sustains carbon sinks under warming Tibetan permafrost region
abstract:
Aboveground symbiotic nitrogen fixation by legumes provides a critical nitrogen source that supports plant biomass growth and sustains carbon sequestration in warming Tibetan permafrost grasslands, based on nitrogen isotope analyses and ecosystem modeling. 
 Symbiotic nitrogen fixation (SNF) by legumes is a major natural source of reactive nitrogen that supports ecosystem functioning and carbon sequestration. Warming across the Tibetan Plateau alpine permafrost region may trigger substantial shifts in vegetation composition and distribution, yet the consequences for ecosystem nitrogen inputs remain poorly understood. Here, using 1047 plant samples from 323 plots across the Tibetan Plateau and 15N natural-abundance techniques, we quantify legume and non-legume nitrogen sources and regional aboveground SNF rates. Aboveground SNF is tightly linked to legume aboveground biomass, ranges from 0 to 7.43 g N m−2 yr−1, and peaks at elevations of 3600–4000 m. At the regional scale, its spatial distribution largely coincides with recent decadal gains in aboveground biomass and plant nitrogen density. Process-based simulations show that removing SNF causes severe nitrogen limitation and shifts these ecosystems from a carbon sink to a source. Our findings highlight the important role of legumes in sustaining carbon sinks in Tibetan Plateau permafrost ecosystems. Aboveground symbiotic nitrogen fixation by legumes provides a critical nitrogen source that supports plant biomass growth and sustains carbon sequestration in warming Tibetan permafrost grasslands, based on nitrogen isotope analyses and ecosystem modeling.
